subject: general
question: If the length of a resistor is doubled, what happens to its resistance, assuming all other 8 factors remain constant?
solution:
The correct answer is __The resistance is doubled__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Resistance__ is directly proportional to the length of the resistor.
 
• If the length of the resistor is doubled, the resistance will also double.
 
• The formula for resistance is given by R = ρL/A, where:
 __
 
• R = Resistance
 
• ρ = Resistivity of the material (constant for a given material)
 
• L = Length of the resistor
 
• A = Cross-sectional area of the resistor
 
 
 
• Since all other factors remain constant, increasing the length leads to a proportional increase in resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Effect of Area:**

 
 
• If the cross-sectional area of the resistor is increased, the resistance will decrease.
 
• Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area (A).
 
 
 
• **Effect of Material:**
 
 
• The resistivity (ρ) depends on the material of the resistor.
 
• Materials with lower resistivity are better conductors.
 
 
 
• **Temperature Dependence:**
 
 
• Resistance generally increases with temperature for conductors.
 
• For some materials, like semiconductors, resistance can decrease with increasing temperature.
